claim: During locomotion, C. elegans spontaneously cycles between forward runs, reversals, and turns with complex but predictable dynamics.
source: During locomotion, the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans spontaneously cycles between forward runs, reversals, and turns with complex but predictable dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of C. elegans locomotion behavior.

claim: RIM interneurons are active during reversals.
source: Here, we provide insight into these dynamics by demonstrating how RIM interneurons, which are active during reversals, act in two modes to stabilize both forward runs and reversals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work in the introduction.

claim: RIM lengthens reversals when depolarized through glutamate and tyramine neurotransmitters.
source: By systematically quantifying the roles of RIM outputs during spontaneous behavior, we show that RIM lengthens reversals when depolarized through glutamate and tyramine neurotransmitters and lengthens forward runs when hyperpolarized through its gap junctions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-3.

claim: RIM lengthens forward runs when hyperpolarized through its gap junctions.
source: By systematically quantifying the roles of RIM outputs during spontaneous behavior, we show that RIM lengthens reversals when depolarized through glutamate and tyramine neurotransmitters and lengthens forward runs when hyperpolarized through its gap junctions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 5-7.

claim: RIM gap junctions actively reinforce a hyperpolarized state of the reversal circuit when RIM is hyperpolarized.
source: RIM is not merely silent upon hyperpolarization: RIM gap junctions actively reinforce a hyperpolarized state of the reversal circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing effects of gap junction knockdown.

claim: The combined outputs of chemical synapses and gap junctions from RIM regulate forward-to-reversal transitions.
source: Additionally, the combined outputs of chemical synapses and gap junctions from RIM regulate forward-to-reversal transitions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Multiple classes of RIM synapses create behavioral inertia during spontaneous locomotion.
source: Our results indicate that multiple classes of RIM synapses create behavioral inertia during spontaneous locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the combined experimental findings.

claim: C. elegans has locomotion-coupled, global brain activity states.
source: Like many animals, C. elegans has locomotion-coupled, global brain activity states (Kato et al., 2015; Musall et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: AIB, AVA, and RIM interneurons are active when animals reverse.
source: A set of interneurons including AIB, AVA, and RIM are active when animals reverse (Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: AIY, RIB, and AVB interneurons are active during forward runs.
source: a different set, AIY, RIB, and AVB, are active during forward runs (Kaplan et al., 2020; Kato et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: AIB, RIB, and RIV are active during sharp omega turns, which typically follow a reversal.
source: and a set including AIB, RIB, and RIV are active during sharp omega turns, which typically follow a reversal (Kato et al., 2015; Nguyen et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: AVA neurons are backward command neurons that drive reversals.
source: The AVA neurons, for example, are backward command neurons that drive reversals; when AVA neurons are optogenetically depolarized, animals reverse, and when AVA neurons are ablated or acutely silenced reversals are short and infrequent (Chalfie et al., 1985; Gordus et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Pokala et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: When AVA neurons are optogenetically depolarized, animals reverse.
source: when AVA neurons are optogenetically depolarized, animals reverse, and when AVA neurons are ablated or acutely silenced reversals are short and infrequent (Chalfie et al., 1985; Gordus et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Pokala et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: When AVA neurons are ablated or acutely silenced, reversals are short and infrequent.
source: when AVA neurons are optogenetically depolarized, animals reverse, and when AVA neurons are ablated or acutely silenced reversals are short and infrequent (Chalfie et al., 1985; Gordus et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Pokala et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Acute silencing of AVA often causes aberrant pauses followed by a turn.
source: Acute silencing of AVA often causes aberrant pauses – thwarted reversals – followed by a turn, indicating that AVA neurons are required for the execution of a reversal, but not for the global dynamics of the forward-reversal-turn sequence (Kato et al., 2015; Pokala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: AVA neurons are required for the execution of a reversal, but not for the global dynamics of the forward-reversal-turn sequence.
source: Acute silencing of AVA often causes aberrant pauses – thwarted reversals – followed by a turn, indicating that AVA neurons are required for the execution of a reversal, but not for the global dynamics of the forward-reversal-turn sequence (Kato et al., 2015; Pokala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from experimental observations with supporting citations.

claim: RIM is active during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked reversals.
source: RIM is active during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked reversals, and its activity correlates with reversal speed (Gordus et al., 2015; Kagawa-Nagamura et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM activity correlates with reversal speed.
source: RIM is active during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked reversals, and its activity correlates with reversal speed (Gordus et al., 2015; Kagawa-Nagamura et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM releases the neurotransmitter tyramine.
source: RIM releases the neurotransmitter tyramine, which extends reversals by inhibiting the AVB forward-active neurons and suppresses head oscillations by inhibiting the head muscles, in both cases through the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55 (Alkema et al., 2005; Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM tyramine extends reversals by inhibiting the AVB forward-active neurons through the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55.
source: RIM releases the neurotransmitter tyramine, which extends reversals by inhibiting the AVB forward-active neurons and suppresses head oscillations by inhibiting the head muscles, in both cases through the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55 (Alkema et al., 2005; Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM tyramine suppresses head oscillations by inhibiting the head muscles through the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55.
source: RIM releases the neurotransmitter tyramine, which extends reversals by inhibiting the AVB forward-active neurons and suppresses head oscillations by inhibiting the head muscles, in both cases through the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55 (Alkema et al., 2005; Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM tyramine sharpens reversal-coupled omega turns by activating SER-2, a G protein-coupled receptor on motor neurons.
source: RIM tyramine also sharpens reversal-coupled omega turns by activating SER-2, a G protein-coupled receptor on motor neurons (Donnelly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Optogenetic depolarization of RIM drives reversals.
source: Optogenetic depolarization of RIM drives reversals, but ablation of RIM paradoxically increases spontaneous reversals, indicating that RIM can either induce or suppress reversals (Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2009; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Ablation of RIM paradoxically increases spontaneous reversals.
source: Optogenetic depolarization of RIM drives reversals, but ablation of RIM paradoxically increases spontaneous reversals, indicating that RIM can either induce or suppress reversals (Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2009; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM can either induce or suppress reversals.
source: Optogenetic depolarization of RIM drives reversals, but ablation of RIM paradoxically increases spontaneous reversals, indicating that RIM can either induce or suppress reversals (Gordus et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2009; López-Cruz et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from experimental observations with supporting citations.

claim: RIM expresses the vesicular glutamate transporter EAT-4, identifying it as one of the 38 classes of glutamatergic neurons in C. elegans.
source: In addition to tyramine, RIM expresses the vesicular glutamate transporter EAT-4, identifying it as one of the 38 classes of glutamatergic neurons in C. elegans (Lee et al., 1999; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM forms gap junctions with AIB, AVA, AVE, RIS, and AIY neurons.
source: RIM also forms gap junctions with multiple neurons whose activity is associated with reversals (AIB, AVA, AVE), as well as neurons active during pauses (RIS) and forward runs (AIY) (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Animals lacking RIM glutamate had an increased frequency of reversals during local search, but not global search.
source: The resulting animals lacking RIM glutamate had an increased frequency of reversals during local search, but not global search (Figures 1E and 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 2A-B.

claim: tdc-1 mutants had an increased reversal frequency during local search.
source: As previously reported, tdc-1 mutants had an increased reversal frequency during local search (Figures 1E and 2A and B; Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation and supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 2A-B.

claim: RIM is the primary neuronal source of tyramine.
source: RIM is the primary neuronal source of tyramine, whose synthesis requires the tyrosine decarboxylase encoded by tdc-1 (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Tyramine synthesis requires the tyrosine decarboxylase encoded by tdc-1.
source: RIM is the primary neuronal source of tyramine, whose synthesis requires the tyrosine decarboxylase encoded by tdc-1 (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: tbh-1 did not affect reversal frequency during local search, identifying tyramine as the relevant transmitter for reversals.
source: tbh-1 did not affect reversal frequency during local search, identifying tyramine as the relevant transmitter for reversals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both short and long reversals increased in frequency in RIM glu KO animals during local search.
source: Using these criteria, both short and long reversals increased in frequency in RIM glu KO animals during local search, but only short reversals increased in frequency in tdc-1 mutants or the RIM glu KO; tdc-1 double mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only short reversals increased in frequency in tdc-1 mutants during local search.
source: Using these criteria, both short and long reversals increased in frequency in RIM glu KO animals during local search, but only short reversals increased in frequency in tdc-1 mutants or the RIM glu KO; tdc-1 double mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Both RIM glu KO animals and tdc-1 mutants had decreased reversal lengths compared to WT.
source: In fact, both RIM glu KO animals and tdc-1 mutants had decreased reversal lengths compared to WT, with a stronger effect in tdc-1 mutants, indicating that RIM glutamate and tyramine both extend reversal length.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RIM glutamate and tyramine both extend reversal length.
source: In fact, both RIM glu KO animals and tdc-1 mutants had decreased reversal lengths compared to WT, with a stronger effect in tdc-1 mutants, indicating that RIM glutamate and tyramine both extend reversal length.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Long reversals are more likely to be followed by an omega turn than short reversals.
source: Long reversals are more likely to be followed by an omega turn than short reversals (Chalasani et al., 2007; Croll, 2009; Gray et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2003; Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: The fraction of reversal-omega maneuvers was reduced in tdc-1 mutants.
source: The fraction of reversal-omega maneuvers was reduced in tdc-1 mutants (Figure 2G, left), while pure reversals that terminate in an immediate forward run increased (Figure 2G, right)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Pure reversals that terminate in an immediate forward run increased in tdc-1 mutants.
source: The fraction of reversal-omega maneuvers was reduced in tdc-1 mutants (Figure 2G, left), while pure reversals that terminate in an immediate forward run increased (Figure 2G, right)
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Omega turn angles were shallower in tdc-1 mutants.
source: as previously reported, omega turn angles were also shallower in tdc-1 mutants (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: RIM glu KO animals had normal reversal-omega frequencies and turn angles after reversals, despite a decrease in reversal length.
source: RIM glu KO animals had normal reversal-omega frequencies and turn angles after reversals, despite a decrease in reversal length (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 2G and H.

claim: Reversal speeds were substantially reduced only in tdc-1 mutants.
source: First, while reversal lengths were decreased in a graded fashion by RIM glu KO or tdc-1 (Figures 2E and 3A), reversal speeds were substantially reduced only in tdc-1 mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: tdc-1 and RIM glu KO had similar decreases in reversal durations.
source: tdc-1 and RIM glu KO had similar decreases in reversal durations (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The RIM glu KO decreased reversal-omega duration but did not affect pure reversal duration.
source: Separating different classes of reversals (Figure 2F and G) revealed that the RIM glu KO decreased reversal-omega duration but did not affect pure reversal duration (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 3D-I.

claim: tdc-1 mutants decreased the duration of reversal-omegas, increased the duration of pure reversals, and decreased the speed of all reversals.
source: tdc-1 mutants decreased the duration of reversal-omegas, increased the duration of pure reversals, and decreased the speed of all reversals (Figure 3D–I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 3D-I.

claim: Pure reversals and reversal-omega maneuvers have distinct kinetics and circuit requirements.
source: These results are in agreement with previous work showing that pure reversals and reversal-omega maneuvers have distinct kinetics and circuit requirements (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Forward runs have an exponential distribution of durations.
source: Forward runs are heterogeneous compared to reversals, with an exponential distribution of durations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Wakabayashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither RIM glu KO animals nor tdc-1 mutants had strong effects on forward run durations compared to controls.
source: Neither RIM glu KO animals nor tdc-1 mutants had strong effects on forward run durations compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both tdc-1 and tbh-1 mutants had substantially diminished forward speeds.
source: Both tdc-1 and tbh-1 mutants had substantially diminished forward speeds, suggesting a role of octopamine in forward locomotion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Tyramine affects both the speed and the duration of all classes of reversals.
source: In summary, tyramine affects both the speed and the duration of all classes of reversals, whereas RIM glutamate only increases the duration of reversals that are coupled to omega turns.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIM glutamate only increases the duration of reversals that are coupled to omega turns.
source: In summary, tyramine affects both the speed and the duration of all classes of reversals, whereas RIM glutamate only increases the duration of reversals that are coupled to omega turns.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIM neurotransmitters do not substantially affect forward run durations.
source: RIM neurotransmitters do not substantially affect forward run durations, consistent with low RIM activity during forward runs.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIC octopamine increases forward and reversal speed.
source: RIC octopamine increases forward and reversal speed.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIM expresses multiple neuropeptides (flp-18, pdf-2, and others).
source: In addition to glutamate and tyramine, RIM expresses multiple neuropeptides (flp-18, pdf-2, and others) (Bhardwaj et al., 2018; Ghosh et al., 2016; Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Release of both classical transmitters and neuropeptides is inhibited by the tetanus toxin light chain.
source: Release of both classical transmitters and neuropeptides is inhibited by the tetanus toxin light chain, which cleaves the synaptic vesicle fusion protein synaptobrevin (Schiavo et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of tetanus toxin in RIM and RIC under the tdc-1 promoter resulted in defects resembling those of tdc-1 mutants.
source: Expression of tetanus toxin in RIM and RIC under the tdc-1 promoter resulted in defects resembling those of tdc-1 mutants (Figure 4A–C): reversal frequency increased, while reversal length, speed, and durations decreased, during local search behavior (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 4A-G.

claim: Expression of tetanus toxin in RIC alone caused only minor defects in reversal frequency and speed.
source: Efficient RIM-only promoters are not available, but expression of tetanus toxin in RIC alone caused only minor defects in reversal frequency and speed, implicating RIM as a major regulator of reversal parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: RIM is a major regulator of reversal parameters.
source: Efficient RIM-only promoters are not available, but expression of tetanus toxin in RIC alone caused only minor defects in reversal frequency and speed, implicating RIM as a major regulator of reversal parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The expression of tetanus toxin in RIM and RIC also increased reversals during the global search period.
source: The expression of tetanus toxin in RIM and RIC also increased reversals during the global search period, an effect that was not observed in RIM glutamate KO or tyramine-deficient mutants (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 4A and C.

claim: Tetanus toxin expression in RIC alone did not affect reversal frequency during global search.
source: Tetanus toxin expression in RIC alone did not affect reversal frequency during global search (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Another transmitter from RIM, perhaps a neuropeptide, suppresses reversals during global search.
source: These results suggest that another transmitter from RIM, perhaps a neuropeptide, suppresses reversals during global search.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Silencing RIM with HisCl led to a substantial decrease in spontaneous reversal frequency, which was most evident during local search.
source: Unexpectedly, silencing RIM with HisCl led to a substantial decrease in spontaneous reversal frequency, which was most evident during local search (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The effects of RIM silencing on reversal frequency were opposite to those of RIM ablation, RIM neurotransmitter mutants, or RIM::tetanus toxin expression.
source: The effects on reversal frequency were opposite to those of RIM ablation, RIM neurotransmitter mutants, or RIM::tetanus toxin expression, all of which increased spontaneous reversal frequency (Alkema et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2005; Figures 2—4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison of data across multiple figures.

claim: The decrease in reversals upon RIM silencing was accompanied by an increase in forward run durations.
source: The decrease in reversals was accompanied by an increase in forward run durations (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RIM has active functions when hyperpolarized that stabilize and extend forward runs.
source: The opposite effects of RIM ablation and acute silencing suggest that RIM has active functions when hyperpolarized that stabilize and extend forward runs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Reversal length, speed, and duration were greatly reduced by hyperpolarization of RIM.
source: Reversal length, speed, and duration were greatly reduced by hyperpolarization of RIM, effects that were similar to but stronger than the effect of tdc-1 or tetanus toxin (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: RIM glutamate and tyramine are released when RIM is depolarized to extend reversals and increase reversal speed.
source: These results suggest that RIM glutamate and tyramine are released when RIM is depolarized, as expected, to extend reversals and increase reversal speed.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Chronic histamine treatment caused decreases in reversal frequency, reversal length, and reversal speed that were similar to those in acutely treated animals.
source: Chronic histamine treatment caused decreases in reversal frequency, reversal length, and reversal speed that were similar to those in acutely treated animals (Figure 5F–H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 5F-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acute RIM silencing decreased the fraction of time that AVA activity was high and reduced spontaneous AVA transitions from the low- to the high-activity state.
source: Acute RIM silencing decreased the fraction of time that AVA activity was high and reduced spontaneous AVA transitions from the low- to the high-activity state (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: RIM hyperpolarization acutely suppresses AVA activity.
source: These results are consistent with a model in which RIM hyperpolarization acutely suppresses AVA activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: RIM shares the most gap junctions with AVA and AVE.
source: RIM shares the most gap junctions with AVA and AVE that, like RIM, have high activity during reversals and low activity during forward runs.
evidence: This is stated based on known anatomical data.

claim: RIM gap junctions stabilize the forward motor state by propagating hyperpolarizing currents between RIM and AVA neurons.
source: We hypothesized that RIM gap junctions stabilize the forward motor state by propagating hyperpolarizing currents between RIM and AVA (and possibly other) neurons, thereby preventing their depolarization.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the experimental data.

claim: RIM neurons express 11 innexin genes, including unc-9.
source: Most C. elegans neurons express multiple innexin genes; RIM neurons express 11 innexin genes, including unc-9 (Bhattacharya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: unc-9 is expressed in many classes of neurons, and mutants have strong defects in forward and backward locomotion.
source: unc-9 is expressed in many classes of neurons, and mutants have strong defects in forward and backward locomotion (Brenner, 1974; Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2006; Park and Horvitz, 1986; Shui et al., 2020; Starich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: RIM gap junction knockdown animals had a greatly increased frequency of reversals compared to WT.
source: However, these gap junction knockdown animals had a greatly increased frequency of reversals compared to WT (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: Both short and long reversals were increased in frequency during both local search and global search in RIM gap junction knockdown animals.
source: Both short and long reversals were increased in frequency during both local search and global search, while reversal length, speed, and duration were only slightly reduced (Figure 6C–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 6C-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RIM gap junction knockdown resulted in a substantial decrease in forward run duration.
source: The RIM gap junction knockdown also resulted in a substantial decrease in forward run duration (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Combining the gap junction knockdown with a tdc-1 mutation yielded additive effects, with both forward and reversal parameters altered.
source: Combining the gap junction knockdown with a tdc-1 mutation yielded additive effects, with both forward and reversal parameters altered (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Knocking down UNC-9 gap junctions in RIC alone did not affect reversal frequency, but decreased both forward speed and reversal speed, as well as forward run duration.
source: Knocking down UNC-9 gap junctions in RIC alone did not affect reversal frequency, but decreased both forward speed and reversal speed, as well as forward run duration (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: unc-9-containing gap junctions in RIM promote forward locomotion.
source: These results support the hypothesis that unc-9-containing gap junctions in RIM promote forward locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Combining the RIM gap junction knockdown with RIM hyperpolarization resulted in mutual suppression of their effect on reversal frequency.
source: Combining the RIM gap junction knockdown with RIM hyperpolarization resulted in mutual suppression of their effect on reversal frequency, so that double mutants had a similar reversal frequency to wild-type animals (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 7A and B.

claim: The shortened forward run durations observed in RIM gap junction knockdown animals were suppressed when RIM was hyperpolarized.
source: The shortened forward run durations observed in RIM gap junction knockdown animals were also suppressed when RIM was hyperpolarized (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Forward states are stabilized in part, but not entirely, through unc-9-containing gap junctions.
source: These results suggest that forward states are stabilized in part, but not entirely, through unc-9-containing gap junctions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The frequency of optogenetically induced reversals was unaffected by tdc-1, RIM glu KO, or the double mutant.
source: The frequency of optogenetically induced reversals was unaffected by tdc-1, RIM glu KO, or the double mutant, whether examined during local search or during global search (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: RIM does not require tyramine or glutamate neurotransmitters to trigger optogenetically induced reversals.
source: This result suggests that RIM does not require tyramine or glutamate neurotransmitters to trigger optogenetically induced reversals.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The RIM gap junction knockdown did not affect optogenetically induced reversal frequencies during local search, but it did decrease optogenetically induced reversals during global search.
source: The RIM gap junction knockdown did not affect optogenetically induced reversal frequencies during local search, but it did decrease optogenetically induced reversals during global search (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: unc-9 gap junctions have a minor role in the initiation of optogenetically induced reversals.
source: These results suggest a minor role for unc-9 gap junctions in the initiation of optogenetically induced reversals.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Optogenetically induced reversals were shorter in RIM glu KO, tyramine-deficient, and RIM gap junction knockdown animals than in WT.
source: Optogenetically induced reversals were shorter in RIM glu KO, tyramine-deficient, and RIM gap junction knockdown animals than in WT (Figure 7E and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 7E and G.

claim: Optogenetically induced reversals are extended by all RIM synaptic outputs.
source: Thus, optogenetically induced reversals are extended by all RIM synaptic outputs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: RIM generates behavioral inertia to inform the dynamics of locomotor states.
source: We show here that RIM generates behavioral inertia to inform the dynamics of these locomotor states (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: RIM stabilizes reversals through its chemical synapses while depolarized and stabilizes forward runs through its gap junctions while hyperpolarized.
source: RIM stabilizes reversals through its chemical synapses while depolarized and stabilizes forward runs through its gap junctions while hyperpolarized.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Hyperpolarization through gap junctions is a recurrent circuit motif in C. elegans locomotion.
source: Together with other results (Kawano et al., 2011), our results suggest that hyperpolarization through gap junctions is a recurrent circuit motif in C. elegans locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data combined with previous work.

claim: When removed from food and placed on a featureless agar surface, C. elegans engages in local search, in which a high frequency of spontaneous reversals limits dispersal from the recently encountered food source.
source: When removed from food and placed on a featureless agar surface, C. elegans engages in local search, in which a high frequency of spontaneous reversals limits dispersal from the recently encountered food source.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral assay used.

claim: Over about 15 min, animals spontaneously transition into global search, a state with infrequent reversals and long forward runs that promotes dispersal.
source: Over about 15 min, animals spontaneously transition into global search, a state with infrequent reversals and long forward runs that promotes dispersal (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the behavioral assay and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: C. elegans mutants lacking the vesicular glutamate transporter eat-4 or various glutamate receptors have abnormal local search behaviors.
source: C. elegans mutants lacking the vesicular glutamate transporter eat-4 or various glutamate receptors have abnormal local search behaviors (Baidya et al., 2014; Chalasani et al., 2007; Choi et al., 2015; Hills et al., 2004; López-Cruz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: The intersection of tdc-1 and eat-4 expression is limited to RIM.
source: The intersection of tdc-1 and eat-4 expression is limited to RIM, leading to excision of the eat-4 ORF in RIM, confirmed by mCherry expression in the targeted cells.
evidence: This is stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and confirmed by imaging data.

claim: Reversals during local search segregate into short reversals of less than half a body length, and long reversals that average >1 body length.
source: Reversals during local search segregate into short reversals of less than half a body length, and long reversals that average >1 body length (Gray et al., 2005; Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and shown in Figures 2C and D.

claim: RIM glutamate and tyramine both inhibit reversal initiation.
source: All of these synaptic outputs inhibit reversal initiation, even though RIM glutamate and tyramine stabilize the reversal once it has begun.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Among the characterized neurons within the foraging circuit, RIM is the only neuron where ablation has opposite effects on the initiation and execution of a behavioral state.
source: Among the characterized neurons within the foraging circuit, RIM is the only neuron where ablation has opposite effects on the initiation and execution of a behavioral state (Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Tyramine release during learning can lead to long-term circuit remodeling.
source: Tyramine release during learning can lead to long-term circuit remodeling, and tyramine mediates systemic responses to starvation and other stresses (De Rosa et al., 2019; Ghosh et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2016; Özbey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Reversal frequencies during local search are regulated by prior experience on bacterial food, including its density and distribution.
source: Reversal frequencies during local search are regulated by prior experience on bacterial food, including its density and distribution (Calhoun et al., 2014; López-Cruz et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Neurons that release both classical transmitters and biogenic amines can employ them additively, cooperatively, or distinctly.
source: Neurons that release both classical transmitters, like glutamate, and biogenic amines, like tyramine, can employ them additively, cooperatively, or distinctly.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about neurotransmitter co-release.

claim: In mice, dopaminergic neurons that project from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens release both dopamine and glutamate, and either transmitter can support positive reinforcement.
source: In mice, dopaminergic neurons that project from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens release both dopamine and glutamate, and either transmitter can support positive reinforcement (Zell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: In both Drosophila and mice, the glutamate transporter enhances dopamine loading into synaptic vesicles for a cooperative effect.
source: In both Drosophila and mice, the glutamate transporter enhances dopamine loading into synaptic vesicles for a cooperative effect (Aguilar et al., 2017; Münster-Wandowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: GABA and dopamine co-released from terminals in the mammalian striatum affect target neurons differently – GABA rapidly inhibits action potentials, while dopamine modulates activity through slower GPCR pathways.
source: At a more subtle level, GABA and dopamine co-released from terminals in the mammalian striatum affect target neurons differently – GABA rapidly inhibits action potentials, while dopamine modulates activity through slower GPCR pathways (Tritsch and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: The nonadditive effects of RIM glutamate and tyramine on spontaneous and optogenetically evoked behavioral dynamics suggest that they act as co-transmitters to cooperatively stabilize reversal states when RIM is depolarized.
source: The nonadditive effects of RIM glutamate and tyramine on spontaneous and optogenetically evoked behavioral dynamics in C. elegans suggest that they act as co-transmitters to cooperatively stabilize reversal states when RIM is depolarized.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The AIB and AVA reversal-promoting neurons express excitatory AMPA-type glutamate receptors.
source: Among RIM's synaptic targets, the AIB and AVA reversal-promoting neurons express excitatory AMPA-type glutamate receptors, as does RIM itself (Brockie et al., 2001; Hart et al., 1995; Taylor et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Glutamate is released onto AVA during reversals.
source: and glutamate is released onto AVA during reversals (Marvin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: RIM glutamate might reinforce the reversal state by depolarizing AVA, while RIM tyramine inhibits the competing forward state via the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55 on AVB.
source: RIM glutamate might reinforce the reversal state by depolarizing AVA, while RIM tyramine inhibits the competing forward state via the tyramine-gated chloride channel LGC-55 on AVB (Pirri et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on known receptor expression and function.

claim: AVA expresses a glutamate-gated chloride channel, avr-14, that inhibits spontaneous reversals.
source: AVA also expresses a glutamate-gated chloride channel, avr-14, that inhibits spontaneous reversals; a genetic interaction between avr-14 and an RIM-specific knockdown of eat-4 suggests that this receptor could be a target of RIM glutamate (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Genetic inactivation of gap junctions between AVA and VA/DA motor neurons results in defects in forward locomotion and increases calcium levels in AVA.
source: Genetic inactivation of those gap junctions results in defects in forward locomotion and increases calcium levels in AVA (Kawano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: The UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions between AVA and VA/DA motor neurons were inferred to decrease the activity of AVA based on hyperpolarizing current flow from VA and DA motor neurons.
source: From this result, the UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions were inferred to decrease the activity of AVA based on hyperpolarizing current flow from VA and DA motor neurons.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from previous work.

claim: The unc-9 innexin expressed in VA/DA neurons and RIM can form heterotypic gap junctions with the unc-7 innexin expressed in AVA.
source: In fact, it could be molecularly similar: the unc-9 innexin expressed in VA/DA neurons and RIM can form heterotypic gap junctions with the unc-7 innexin expressed in AVA (Kawano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Direct measurements of gap junctions between AVA and VA5 motor neurons indicate that UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions transmit depolarizing current from VA5 to AVA.
source: Moreover, direct measurements of gap junctions between AVA and VA5 motor neurons indicate that UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions transmit depolarizing current from VA5 to AVA (Liu et al., 2017; Shui et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Reconstitution in Xenopus oocytes revealed a startling array of rectifying and membrane potential-dependent properties of UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions, depending on which of the seven UNC-7 splice forms is expressed.
source: That said, reconstitution in Xenopus oocytes revealed a startling array of rectifying and membrane potential-dependent properties of UNC-9-UNC-7 gap junctions, depending on which of the seven UNC-7 splice forms is expressed (Shui et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Interactions between chemical and electrical synapses play prominent roles in motor circuits including the stomatogastric ganglion of crustaceans, the heartbeat circuit in leeches, and rapid escape circuits in nematodes, arthropods, and fish.
source: Interactions between chemical and electrical synapses play prominent roles in motor circuits including the stomatogastric ganglion of crustaceans, the heartbeat circuit in leeches, and rapid escape circuits in nematodes, arthropods, and fish (Kristan et al., 2005; Marder, 1998; Szczupak, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Antagonism between electrical and chemical synapses has been observed in the reversal-to-omega-turn transition in C. elegans.
source: Antagonism between electrical and chemical synapses has also been observed in the reversal-to-omega-turn transition in C. elegans (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: Electrical synapses in motor circuits have all been thought to be excitatory.
source: Although chemical synapses in these circuits can be either excitatory or inhibitory, their electrical synapses have all been thought to be excitatory.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about electrical synapses.

claim: Inhibitory electrical synapses resembling those of RIM gap junctions may emerge as stabilizing elements of other motor circuits with long-lasting, mutually exclusive states.
source: We speculate that inhibitory electrical synapses resembling those of RIM gap junctions may emerge as stabilizing elements of other motor circuits with long-lasting, mutually exclusive states.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings.

claim: RIM expresses 11 innexin genes, the most of any neuron.
source: RIM expresses 11 innexin genes, the most of any neuron (Bhattacharya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to previous work.

claim: RIM gap junctions may depolarize AVA via innexins that are not affected by the unc-1(dn) transgene, such as inx-1.
source: RIM gap junctions may depolarize AVA via innexins that are not affected by the unc-1(dn) transgene, such as inx-1 (Hori et al., 2018), which synergizes with unc-9 to promote reversals evoked by optogenetic RIM depolarization (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on previous work.
